accuracy.evidence: Checked against KS1 Working scientifically (asking simple questions and recognising that they can be answered in different ways) and NGSS K-2-ETS1-1. The three ways map to the KS1 enquiry types: observing over time, simple comparative tests and secondary research. Frog timings follow the common frog: tadpoles hatch after about 2 weeks, back legs at about 6-9 weeks, froglets at about 12-16 weeks, so the lab says 'about'. Moon distance 384,400 km average (NASA), shown as about 384,000 km. Bounce heights are described in words, with tennis ball about half (ITF rebound 135-147 cm from 254 cm).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips for 5-7 year olds in enquiry: treating a guess as finding out, one look at a slow change, trying to test or measure things that are too far away (a ruler for the Moon), assuming 'the biggest ball must bounce highest' without testing, and treating a preference ('which colour is best?') as a science question.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagsciq is about how a question gets answered: a garden of question prompts, a frog tank watched over 12 weeks, a same-height ball drop test, a book look-up for the Moon, a sort of questions into watch/test/look it up, and a 'science cannot answer this' card choice. flagask and flagfind are about asking people for help in daily life and flagobs separates seeing from interpreting; none has enquiry types. Shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner finds out each way by doing it before being told: frogspawn only becomes a frog after four looks spread over weeks, the bouncy ball only proves highest once all three balls are dropped from the same dashed line, and the Moon distance only comes from the book. The sort step then makes them choose the way for new questions, with feedback on each wrong choice.

predictions.evidence: Six predictions, each led by a tempting wrong option: 'only grown-ups can ask', 'make a guess', 'the biggest ball, for sure', 'measure it with a ruler', 'look it up only' for the plant test, and 'yes, test all the ice creams'. The reveal names the child's own choice.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge questions; wrong answers are tagged book, slow, once, guess, far or like and each has its own short message: we can try this ourselves, this is quick to test, growing needs many looks, a guess is not finding out, too far to test so look it up, and 'nicest' is what you like.

readability.evidence: Kid text Flesch-Kincaid grade 1.3 (family target ≤ 5); words are short and concrete (watch, test, look it up, frogspawn, ball, Moon). Lab text is one or two short sentences per step. The young layout gives 56 px buttons and larger step text. Adult text grade 7.0 (target ≤ 10).

no_filler.evidence: Content gate passed with no filler phrases. Each kid paragraph has one job: what a science question is, finding out by watching, finding out by testing or looking it up, and questions science cannot answer. Adult text gives curriculum placement, the enquiry types, mistakes and what the lab does.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 screenshots in both themes: the four garden tiles, frog tank, three balls with labels, Moon picture and three sort bins fit the 390 px canvas with no clipped text; every control is a large young-layout button, and the button rows wrap without overflow. Emoji are drawn at full opacity after the fix.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas tap has a labelled button: four 'Ask about the …' buttons, Look again later, three Drop buttons, Look it up, three 'Find out by …' buttons and the three question cards. The canvas aria-label is rewritten with each new question, stage or result. walk.cjs axe WCAG 2.1 AA was clean in both themes on desktop and phone.
